summary.text: After removing the multiples of \(p\) from the factorial ratios and pairing each remaining residue with its complement modulo \(p^r\), the shifted products are expanded in powers of \(p^{2r}\); inversion symmetry and quadratic/fourth-power sums show that the first symmetric coefficient is divisible by \(p^r\) (by \(3^{r-1}\) when \(p=3\)) and the second by \(p\) for \(p\ge5\). A telescoped binomial congruence gives the additional factor \(p^3\) in \(2\binom{3p^{r-1}}{p^{r-1}}^2-9\binom{2p^{r-1}}{p^{r-1}}\) (using the explicit base values for \(p=3\)); these bounds make every surviving expansion term divisible by \(p^{3r+3}\), after which the product over \(p\)-units is cancelled.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\binom{3n}{n}^{2}-27\binom{2n}{n}.
\]
Fix a prime \(p\ge 3\) and an integer \(r\ge2\). Put
\[
P=p^r,\qquad n=p^{r-1},\qquad M=p^{3r+3}.
\]
We prove that \(M\mid a(P)-a(n)\).

Throughout the proof, congruences and divisibilities are in the integers.

## 1. Products with the multiples of \(p\) removed

For a positive integer \(X\), define
\[
\Pi^*(X)=\prod_{\substack{1\le m\le X\\p\nmid m}}m.
\]
If \(p\mid Q\), and \(T\ge0\), also define
\[
W_t(Q)=\prod_{\substack{1\le k\le Q\\p\nmid k}}(tQ+k).
\]
Thus \(W_0(Q)=\Pi^*(Q)\). Splitting the factors in \((Q+R)!\) at \(Q\), whenever \(p\mid Q\), gives the telescoping identity
\[
\Pi^*(Q+R)=\Pi^*(Q)\prod_{\substack{1\le k\le R\\p\nmid k}}(Q+k).
\]
In particular,
\[
\Pi^*(2Q)=\Pi^*(Q)W_1(Q),\qquad
\Pi^*(3Q)=\Pi^*(2Q)W_2(Q).
\]

We also have the elementary factorial decomposition
\[
X!=\Pi^*(X)\,p^{\lfloor X/p\rfloor}\left\lfloor\frac Xp\right\rfloor!.
\tag{1}
\]
Indeed, the factors divisible by \(p\) in \(1,\ldots,X\) are precisely
\(p,2p,\ldots,\lfloor X/p\rfloor p\), whose product is
\(p^{\lfloor X/p\rfloor}\lfloor X/p\rfloor!\).

Apply (1) to \(Q=pn\), \(2Q\), and \(3Q\), and use the usual factorial formulas for binomial coefficients. After cancelling the common positive factorial factors, one obtains
\[
\Pi^*(Q)\binom{3Q}{Q}=\binom{3n}{n}W_2(Q),
\tag{2}
\]
and
\[
\Pi^*(Q)\binom{2Q}{Q}=\binom{2n}{n}W_1(Q).
\tag{3}
\]
For our \(Q=P=pn\), write
\[
W=W_0(P)=\Pi^*(P),\qquad
A=\binom{3n}{n},\qquad B=\binom{2n}{n}.
\]
Then (2) and (3) become
\[
W\binom{3P}{P}=A W_2(P),
\qquad
W\binom{2P}{P}=B W_1(P).
\tag{4}
\]
Every factor of \(W\) is prime to \(p\), so
\[
\gcd(W,p)=1.
\tag{5}
\]

## 2. Pairing the factors in \(W_t(P)\)

Let
\[
U(P)=\{k:1\le k\le P,\ p\nmid k\}
\]
and choose the lower member from each pair \(\{k,P-k\}\):
\[
L(P)=\{\ell:1\le \ell\le P,\ p\nmid\ell,\ 2\ell<P\}.
\]
Since \(p\) is odd and \(p\mid P\), the map \(\ell\mapsto P-\ell\) bijects \(L(P)\) with the complementary upper half of \(U(P)\). There is no fixed point: if \(2\ell=P\), primality of \(p\) would force \(p\mid2\) or \(p\mid\ell\), both impossible.

Pairing corresponding factors gives
\[
(tP+\ell)(tP+P-\ell)
=\ell(P-\ell)+t(t+1)P^2.
\]
Consequently,
\[
W_t(P)=\prod_{\ell\in L(P)}
\bigl(q_\ell+t(t+1)P^2\bigr),
\qquad q_\ell=\ell(P-\ell).
\tag{6}
\]
Because \(p\ge3\), \(r\ge2\), and hence \(P\ge9\), both \(1\) and \(2\) belong to \(L(P)\). Thus \(|L(P)|\ge2\).

Let \(m=|L(P)|\), and define the two elementary symmetric expressions
\[
S_1=\sum_{\ell\in L(P)}\prod_{j\in L(P)\setminus\{\ell\}}q_j,
\tag{7}
\]
\[
S_2=\sum_{\substack{T\subseteq L(P)\\|T|=m-2}}\prod_{j\in T}q_j.
\tag{8}
\]
Thus \(S_1\) and \(S_2\) are respectively the elementary symmetric polynomials of degrees \(m-1\) and \(m-2\) in the \(q_\ell\)'s.

For any integer \(c\), expansion of a product gives
\[
\prod_{\ell\in L(P)}(q_\ell+c)
=\prod q_\ell+cS_1+c^2S_2+\sum_{j\ge3}c^j E_{m-j},
\tag{9}
\]
where the remaining \(E_{m-j}\) are integer elementary symmetric expressions. In (6),
\[
c=t(t+1)P^2=t(t+1)p^{2r}.
\]
Since \(c^3\) is divisible by \(p^{6r}\), and \(6r\ge3r+3\) for \(r\ge1\), all terms of degree at least three in (9) vanish modulo \(M\). Therefore
\[
W_t(P)\equiv W+t(t+1)p^{2r}S_1+ igl(t(t+1)p^{2r}\bigr)^2S_2\pmod M.
\tag{10}
\]
In particular, if we put \(e=p^{2r}\), then
\[
W_1(P)\equiv W+2eS_1+4e^2S_2\pmod M,
\tag{11}
\]
\[
W_2(P)\equiv W+6eS_1+36e^2S_2\pmod M.
\tag{12}
\]

We next establish the divisibility properties of \(S_1\) and \(S_2\) needed later.

## 3. A quadratic power sum and the divisibility of \(S_1\)

The sum of the squares of the members of \(U(P)\) can be evaluated by subtracting the multiples of \(p\) from the full sum of squares. Using
\[
6\sum_{x=0}^{N-1}x^2=(N-1)N(2N-1),
\]
with \(P=p^r\), we get
\[
6\sum_{x\in U(P)}x^2
=(P-1)P(2P-1)
-p^2(p^{r-1}-1)p^{r-1}(2p^{r-1}-1).
\]
A direct simplification yields
\[
6\sum_{x\in U(P)}x^2
=p^r(p-1)\bigl(2p^{2r-1}-1\bigr).
\tag{13}
\]
If \(p\ge5\), then \(p\nmid6\), so (13) implies
\[
p^r\mid\sum_{x\in U(P)}x^2.
\tag{14}
\]
If \(p=3\), cancellation of the single factor \(3\) in \(6\) gives instead
\[
3^{r-1}\mid\sum_{x\in U(P)}x^2.
\tag{15}
\]

We now convert these power-sum facts into divisibility of \(S_1\). We use the following general observation. Suppose \(a\le r\) and
\[
p^a\mid\sum_{x\in U(P)}x^2.
\tag{16}
\]
Work modulo \(p^a\). Every member of \(U(P)\) is a unit. Inversion permutes the reduced residues modulo \(P=p^r\), and reduction from modulus \(P\) to modulus \(p^a\) respects inversion. Hence
\[
\sum_{x\in U(P)}x^{-2}=\sum_{x\in U(P)}x^2=0\pmod{p^a}.
\tag{17}
\]
Pairing \(x\) with \(P-x\), and noting that \((P-x)^{-2}=(-x)^{-2}=x^{-2}\) modulo \(p^a\), gives
\[
\sum_{x\in U(P)}x^{-2}
=2\sum_{\ell\in L(P)}\ell^{-2}.
\]
Since \(p\) is odd, \(2\) is invertible modulo \(p^a\), and therefore
\[
\sum_{\ell\in L(P)}\ell^{-2}=0\pmod{p^a}.
\tag{18}
\]

Also, because \(p^a\mid P\),
\[
q_\ell=\ell(P-\ell)\equiv-\ell^2\pmod{p^a}.
\]
Thus each \(q_\ell\) is a unit and
\[
q_\ell^{-1}\equiv-\ell^{-2}\pmod{p^a}.
\]
Using (7), we may factor the complete product of the \(q_\ell\)'s:
\[
S_1=\left(\prod_{j\in L(P)}q_j\right)
\left(\sum_{\ell\in L(P)}q_\ell^{-1}\right).
\tag{19}
\]
By (18), the second factor is zero modulo \(p^a\). Therefore
\[
p^a\mid S_1.
\tag{20}
\]
Combining this with (14) and (15), we obtain
\[
\boxed{p^r\mid S_1\quad(p\ge5)},
\tag{21}
\]
\[
\boxed{3^{r-1}\mid S_1\quad(p=3)}.
\tag{22}
\]

## 4. Divisibility of \(S_2\) for \(p\ge5\)

For this part assume \(p\ge5\). We prove
\[
\boxed{p\mid S_2}.
\tag{23}
\]
Work modulo \(p\). Put \(u_\ell=q_\ell^{-1}\). As above,
\[
u_\ell=-\ell^{-2}.
\tag{24}
\]
Equation (14), reduced modulo \(p\), and the inversion and pairing argument just used show
\[
\sum_{\ell\in L(P)}u_\ell=0\pmod p.
\tag{25}
\]
We also need the sum of the squares of the \(u_\ell\)'s. Every element of \(U(P)\) has a unique expression
\[
x=jp+b,
\qquad 0\le j<p^{r-1},\quad 1\le b<p.
\]
Modulo \(p\), its fourth power is \(b^4\). Hence
\[
\sum_{x\in U(P)}x^4
=p^{r-1}\sum_{b=1}^{p-1}b^4=0\pmod p,
\tag{26}
\]
because \(r\ge2\). Inversion permutes the units and pairing \(x\) with \(P-x\) again divides this even-power sum by \(2\). Thus
\[
\sum_{\ell\in L(P)}\ell^{-4}=0\pmod p.
\]
By (24), this says
\[
\sum_{\ell\in L(P)}u_\ell^2=0\pmod p.
\tag{27}
\]

The elementary identity
\[
2\sum_{\{i,j\}\subseteq L(P)}u_i u_j
=\left(\sum_{i\in L(P)}u_i\right)^2-
\sum_{i\in L(P)}u_i^2
\tag{28}
\]
now shows that the sum over unordered pairs is zero modulo \(p\). On the other hand, factoring the full product of the \(q_\ell\)'s from (8) gives
\[
S_2=\\left(\prod_{\ell\in L(P)}q_\ell\right)
\sum_{\{i,j\}\subseteq L(P)}u_i u_j.
\tag{29}
\]
Equations (25), (27), and (28), together with invertibility of \(2\) modulo \(p\), prove (23).

## 5. A binomial congruence modulo \(p^3\)

We require the auxiliary fact
\[
\boxed{
p^3\mid
2\binom{3p^{r-1}}{p^{r-1}}^2
-9\binom{2p^{r-1}}{p^{r-1}}.
}
\tag{30}
\]
We derive it from the same product identities.

First let \(k\ge2\). Applying (10) with \(P=p^k\), and then reducing modulo \(p^3\), gives
\[
W_t(p^k)\equiv W_0(p^k)\pmod{p^3},
\tag{31}
\]
because the first omitted difference contains \(p^{2k}\), which is divisible by \(p^3\). Apply (2) and (3) with \(Q=p^k=p\cdot p^{k-1}\). Since \(W_0(p^k)\) is prime to \(p\), it can be cancelled modulo \(p^3\). From (31) we get
\[
\binom{3p^k}{p^k}\equiv
\binom{3p^{k-1}}{p^{k-1}}\pmod{p^3},
\tag{32}
\]
\[
\binom{2p^k}{p^k}\equiv
\binom{2p^{k-1}}{p^{k-1}}\pmod{p^3}.
\tag{33}
\]
Iterating from \(k=r-1\) down to \(k=1\) shows that the two binomial coefficients in (30) are congruent modulo \(p^3\) to \(\binom{3p}{p}\) and \(\binom{2p}{p}\), respectively.

Suppose first that \(p\ge5\). The preceding proof of (20), applied with \(P=p\) and \(a=1\), gives \(p\mid S_1\). (Here \(L(p)\) has at least the two elements \(1,2\).) Expanding (6) for \(P=p\) modulo \(p^3\), the linear term contains \(p^2S_1\), and every quadratic or higher term contains at least \(p^4\). Therefore
\[
W_t(p)\equiv W_0(p)\pmod{p^3}.
\]
Using (2) and (3) with \(n=1\), and cancelling the \(p\)-adic unit \(W_0(p)\), gives
\[
\binom{3p}{p}\equiv\binom31=3\pmod{p^3},
\qquad
\binom{2p}{p}\equiv\binom21=2\pmod{p^3}.
\tag{34}
\]
Consequently the expression in (30) is congruent to
\[
2\cdot3^2-9\cdot2=0\pmod{p^3}.
\]

It remains to treat \(p=3\). The iteration (32)–(33) reduces the required expression to the base values
\[
\binom93=84,
\qquad
\binom63=20.
\]
A direct calculation gives
\[
2\cdot84^2-9\cdot20=13932=27\cdot516.
\]
Thus (30) also holds for \(p=3\).

## 6. Expansion of the crucial difference

Recall
\[
A=\binom{3n}{n},\qquad B=\binom{2n}{n},\qquad
W=W_0(P),\qquad e=p^{2r}.
\]
Define
\[
Z=A^2\bigl(W_2(P)^2-W^2\bigr)
-27WB\bigl(W_1(P)-W\bigr).
\tag{35}
\]
Substitute (11) and (12) into this expression. Expanding the resulting polynomial and discarding terms containing \(e^3\) or \(e^4\), which are divisible by \(M\), gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
Z\equiv{}&6eS_1W(2A^2-9B)
+36e^2A^2S_1^2\\
&+36e^2S_2W(2A^2-3B)
\pmod M.
\end{aligned}
\tag{36}
\]
For completeness, before the terms divisible by \(M\) are removed, the exact expansion is
\[
\begin{aligned}
Z={}&6eS_1W(2A^2-9B)
+36e^2A^2S_1^2
+36e^2S_2W(2A^2-3B)\\
&+432A^2S_1S_2e^3+1296A^2S_2^2e^4.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(e^3=p^{6r}\) and \(e^4=p^{8r}\), the last two terms are indeed zero modulo \(p^{3r+3}\).

We now show that each of the three displayed terms in (36) is divisible by \(M\).

### Case 1: \(p\ge5\)

By (21), \(p^r\mid S_1\); by (23), \(p\mid S_2\); and by (30), \(p^3\mid2A^2-9B\). Therefore the first term of (36) contains at least
\[
p^{2r}\cdot p^r\cdot p^3=p^{3r+3}.
\]
The second term contains
\[
e^2S_1^2,
\]
which is divisible by \(p^{4r+2r}=p^{6r}\). Since \(r\ge2\), \(6r\ge3r+3\). The third term contains
\[
e^2S_2,
\]
which is divisible by \(p^{4r+1}\); and
\[
4r+1\ge3r+3
\]
precisely because \(r\ge2\). Hence \(M\mid Z\).

### Case 2: \(p=3\)

Now (22) gives \(3^{r-1}\mid S_1\), while (30) gives \(3^3\mid2A^2-9B\). In addition, the coefficient \(6\) supplies one factor of \(3\). Thus the first term in (36) is divisible by
\[
3^1\cdot3^{2r}\cdot3^{r-1}\cdot3^3=3^{3r+3}.
\]
For the second term, \(36\) supplies \(3^2\), and
\[
36e^2S_1^2
\]
is divisible by
\[
3^{2+4r+2(r-1)}=3^{6r},
\]
which contains \(3^{3r+3}\). Finally, no divisibility of \(S_2\) is needed: the coefficient \(36\) and \(e^2\) already make the third term divisible by
\[
3^{2+4r},
\]
and \(4r+2\ge3r+3\) for \(r\ge1\). Hence again \(M\mid Z\).

Thus in all cases
\[
M\mid Z.
\tag{37}
\]

## 7. Identification of \(Z\) with the desired difference

From (4),
\[
W\binom{3P}{P}=AW_2(P),
\qquad
W\binom{2P}{P}=BW_1(P).
\]
Squaring the first equality and multiplying the second by \(W\), we obtain
\[
W^2\binom{3P}{P}^2=A^2W_2(P)^2,
\qquad
W^2\binom{2P}{P}=WBW_1(P).
\]
Using \(a(P)=\binom{3P}{P}^2-27\binom{2P}{P}\) and
\(a(n)=A^2-27B\), it follows that
\[
\begin{aligned}
W^2(a(P)-a(n))
&=A^2\bigl(W_2(P)^2-W^2\bigr)
 -27WB\bigl(W_1(P)-W\bigr)\\
&=Z.
\end{aligned}
\tag{38}
\]
By (37), \(M\mid W^2(a(P)-a(n))\). But (5) says \(W\) is prime to \(p\), and hence \(W^2\) is prime to \(M=p^{3r+3}\). We may therefore cancel \(W^2\), obtaining
\[
p^{3r+3}\mid a(P)-a(n).
\]
Since \(P=p^r\) and \(n=p^{r-1}\), this is exactly
\[
\boxed{
a(p^r)\equiv a(p^{r-1})\pmod{p^{3r+3}}.
}
\]
This holds for every prime \(p\ge3\) and every \(r\ge2\), as required.
